summary: This CI/CD job sets up SSH authentication to connect to a private GitLab server. It installs necessary tools, configures an SSH key from an encrypted environment variable, registers the server as trusted, and then tests the connection.

explanations.4: The pipe character allows multiple shell commands to be written on separate lines within a single YAML string, rather than on one long line.
explanations.5: This updates the system package list and installs SSH client tools and Git, which are needed to authenticate and clone repositories.
explanations.6: The ssh-agent is a program that holds your SSH key in memory so you don't have to enter your password repeatedly; this command starts it and stores its configuration.
explanations.7: This creates the hidden .ssh directory (if it doesn't exist) and sets its permissions to 700, which means only the owner can read, write, and access it—a security requirement for SSH.
explanations.9: The SSH key is stored in the environment variable as base64-encoded text for security; this line decodes it back to binary and saves it as the private key file that SSH will use.
explanations.11: This restricts the private key file to read-only for the owner (400 permissions), which SSH requires for security—it will refuse to use a key that's too permissive.
explanations.13: This retrieves the public key signature of your GitLab server and adds it to the known_hosts file, so SSH knows it can trust connections to that server without manual verification.
explanations.14: The known_hosts file needs to be readable by SSH but not writable by others, so this sets appropriate permissions (644).
explanations.17: This attempts to connect to the GitLab server and verify that SSH authentication works; the -T flag means it won't execute any commands, just test the connection.
